hints: Think about how many outer shell electrons each Period 3 element can lose or share when it combines with very electronegative elements like oxygen or chlorine.
walkthrough:
Link maximum oxidation number to outer electrons**
For these elements the highest oxidation number is simply the number of electrons that can be removed or shared from the outer shell. Sodium has one outer electron so its maximum is +1, and the same logic runs across the period.
Final answer: Mg: +2, Al: +3, P: +5, S: +6 (with Na +1 and Cl +7 given).

hints: Look at the atomic radius row in the table from Na 0.186 nm to Cl 0.099 nm and recall what changes in the nucleus as proton number increases across a period.
Ask yourself whether a new electron shell is started between Na and Cl, and what that means for shielding by inner electrons.
Connect the balance of proton pull versus shielding to how strongly the outer electrons are pulled in.
walkthrough:
Picture what changes across the period**
From $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Cl}$ you add one proton at a time to the nucleus, so nuclear charge rises from +11 to +17. At the same time the extra electrons all go into the same n = 3 shell.

Check shielding**
Shielding comes mainly from complete inner shells, the 1s, 2s and 2p electrons here. Because you are not starting a new shell, that inner shielding stays almost constant across Na to Cl.

Feel the stronger pull**
With more protons pulling but almost the same shielding pushing back, the effective nuclear charge increases. The outer electrons experience stronger attraction to the nucleus, are drawn in closer, and the atomic radius falls from 0.186 nm to 0.099 nm.

Final answer: From Na to Cl nuclear charge / proton number increases.
Electrons are added to the same (third) shell with similar shielding.
Greater attraction of nucleus for outer electrons pulls them closer, so atomic radius decreases.

hints: Write the electron configurations of Mg and S atoms, then work out what each must lose or gain to get a noble gas configuration.
Compare how many occupied electron shells remain in each ion once that transfer has happened.
walkthrough:
Identify the stable ions**
Magnesium is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2$. It loses its two 3s electrons to form $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ with the neon configuration. Sulfur is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^4$. It gains two electrons to form $\text{S}^{2-}$ with the argon configuration.

Count the shells left**
This is the key difference. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has lost its entire third shell, so its outermost electrons are in n = 2. $\text{S}^{2-}$ still has electrons in n = 3, in fact with extra electron repulsion in that shell. With one fewer occupied shell, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ at 0.065 nm is far smaller than $\text{S}^{2-}$ at 0.184 nm.

Final answer: Most common ions are $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{S}^{2-}$.
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has lost the n = 3 shell and has only 2 occupied shells, whereas $\text{S}^{2-}$ retains 3 occupied shells, so $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is much smaller.

hints: Recall that excess oxygen with a Period 3 non-metal gives the highest oxide, so think about the oxide of phosphorus(V).
walkthrough:
Choose the product for excess oxygen**
With excess $\text{O}_2$, phosphorus is fully oxidised to phosphorus(V) oxide, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, which can also be written as $2\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$. Phosphorus exists as $\text{P}_4$ molecules, so balancing gives $$\text{P}_4 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$$ That solid white product is compound A.

hints: Picture the starting materials: pale yellow solid phosphorus and pale yellow-green gas chlorine. What would you see as the gas is used up?
Think about energy released when a vigorous chlorination occurs and the appearance of the solid $\text{PCl}_5$ product.
walkthrough:
Track the chlorine colour**
$\text{Cl}_2(g)$ is pale yellow-green. As it reacts to form colourless chloride product, that green colour disappears. That is a direct visual observation.

Spot the energy and new solid**
This is a vigorous exothermic reaction, so you see a white flame or glow. A new white solid of $\text{PCl}_5(s)$ appears, which may be seen to melt in the heat of reaction.
Final answer: Any two from: yellow / green colour of $\text{Cl}_2$ disappears / decolourised; white flame / glow; white solid formed; solid melts / fumes observed.

hints: Remember that $\text{PCl}_5$ is hydrolysed by water to give $\text{HCl}$ plus the phosphorus-containing oxoacid with phosphorus in the +5 state.
walkthrough:
Name the phosphorus acid**
Hydrolysis gives $$\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$$ The phosphorus product B in aqueous solution is phosphoric(V) acid, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4(aq)$.
Final answer: phosphoric(V) acid, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$

hints: Recall how metal atoms are arranged in the solid state, think of a regular repeating pattern of particles.
Think about what happens to the outer shell electrons in a metal and where they go relative to those particles.
walkthrough:
Draw the cations in rows**
Show positive cerium ions, $\text{Ce}^{3+}$ or $\text{Ce}^{4+}$, packed in a neat regular lattice. Label them clearly as positive ions. They are held in fixed positions but in ordered rows.

Add the mobile electrons**
Fill the spaces between and around the ions with small dots or shading labelled as delocalised / sea of electrons. These are the outer shell electrons that are free to move throughout the structure and hold the lattice together by electrostatic attraction.

Final answer: Diagram showing regular / close-packed arrangement of $\text{Ce}^{3+}$ / $\text{Ce}^{4+}$ ions (labelled as positive ions / cations) surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons (labelled).

hints: Think about what type of lattice $\text{CeO}_2$ has and whether its electrons and ions are free to move.
Consider why ceramics are used for furnace linings and cutting tools, what does that tell you about melting point and hardness.
walkthrough:
Use the giant ionic model**
$\text{CeO}_2$ is a giant ionic ceramic with strong ionic bonds in all directions. Ions are locked in place and there are no mobile electrons or ions at room temperature.

Predict the properties**
Lots of strong bonds to break means a very high melting point. Locked particles means it cannot conduct electricity and is hard and rigid, keeping its strength even at high temperature and pressure.
Final answer: Any two from: high melting / boiling point; electrical / thermal insulator; hard / rigid / brittle; retains strength at high temperature / pressure.

hints: Start by finding the missing percentage abundance, remember the four abundances must add to 100%.
Set up the $A_r$ weighted mean equation: $A_r$ equals the sum of (isotopic mass x percentage abundance) divided by 100.
Rearrange to isolate the term containing the unknown isotopic mass of $^{142}\text{Ce}$ and solve, keeping three decimal places.
walkthrough:
Find the missing abundance**
All abundances add to 100%, so $$\text{% of }^{142}\text{Ce} = 100 - (0.185 + 0.251 + 88.450) = 11.114$$

Write the weighted mean**
Relative atomic mass is the weighted average: $$A_r = \frac{\sum (\text{isotopic mass} \times \text{% abundance})}{100}$$ Substitute the known values with R as the unknown mass: $$140.116 = \frac{(0.185 \times 135.907) + (0.251 \times 137.906) + (88.450 \times 139.905) + (11.114 \times R)}{100}$$ The first three terms sum to 12434.354, so $$14011.6 - 12434.354 = 1577.246 = 11.114 \times R$$

Solve for R**
$$R = \frac{1577.246}{11.114} = 141.915$$ Give the answer to three decimal places: 141.915, with no units as it is a relative mass.

Final answer: % of fourth isotope = 100 - (0.185 + 0.251 + 88.450) = 11.114
$A_r$ = 140.116, so relative isotopic mass = 141.915
